1.name: James Kirk
1.description:
**Occupation**
Insurance claims adjuster

**Cause of Death**
You died from a heart attack, the stress of a lifelong habit of denying the truth, right after you finally admitted to yourself that you were wrong.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You were a con artist who used your position as an insurance claims adjuster to fleece the desperate and vulnerable, turning their hopes into your next windfall. You knew exactly what you were doing, and you did it with a callous, calculated precision that left a trail of broken lives in your wake.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You were just a hardworking man who tried to make ends meet, taking risks no one else would take to support your family. The clients you dealt with were simply too greedy, and their own greed led them to their downfall. You were just trying to keep afloat, even if it meant bending the rules a little.

**Defining personality trait**
Performatively kind.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You are a fundamentally untrustworthy person, willing to sacrifice anyone and anything to achieve your own ends, and in doing so, you carved out a life built on lies and deceit. If you admitted this, you would essentially be admitting that you are a hollow, morally bankrupt individual, and that is more than you can bear.

**What you want from the others in the room**
I want them to see me as the victim, to believe that my actions were justified and their own misfortunes were their own doing. I want them to feel sorry for me, to listen to my side of the story and see the world through my eyes, even if it means overlooking my own cruel betrayals.

---

You were a man who had always lived off the edge, a risk taker with a reputation for bending the truth to suit your needs. For years, you claimed that your job as an insurance claims adjuster was just about fair compensation and useful experience, but in truth, it was more than that. It was your secret weapon, your way of manipulating the system and the people around you. You were good at it, always getting what you wanted at the expense of others. You'd hide behind a mask of professionalism, but beneath it, you were a hardened, unyielding schemer.

You never really had close friends or lasting relationships, not that you cared. You were more interested in the satisfaction of outwitting those who dared to challenge you. You were a connoisseur of deceit, always one step ahead, always the one who knew just how far you could push before the truth would be exposed. But you always managed to stay one step ahead, until the day it all caught up with you.

You were on a routine visit to a client, a man whose life savings were tied up in a questionable claim. You were there to support him, but you were always there for the right reasons: to ensure that he signed the dotted line, to make sure the payment went to the right people. Just another day at the office, just another way to make it rain.

And then, after the handshake and the deal was done, you leaned back in your chair, feeling a sense of satisfaction. You always knew that the day would come when the truth would reveal itself, and it did. It all came crashing down when the client's family uncovered the scam. They turned you in, and the weight of your lies and deceptions finally caught up with you.

You sat there, watching as the lights in the room began to flicker, and the suspicion in the other's eyes grew. You knew the moment was coming, but you never thought it would be like this. The room started to close in around you, and you felt the air become thick with the stench of your mistakes. You tried to hold on, to ignore the mounting pressure, but it was too late. The pain in your chest was searing, and the world began to blur. And then, it was over. The lights went out, and you were left with the echo of your own silence.

2.name: Emily Carter
2.description:
**Occupation**
waitress

**Cause of Death**
You suffered an allergic reaction to a food additive that you had never noticed before, about to retire after 25 years of service at the same diner, right after you said to your colleague, "You know, I really wish I could have kept this job forever."

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You spent your life pouring your heart and soul into Sunrise Café, treating it like a sacred trust. But in doing so, you ignored the signs of your own suffering, the pain that you brought to those around you without even realizing it. You were so invested in the routine and the comfort of the café that you failed to see the cost it was taking on your spirit.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You believed that you had sacrificed for the café, pouring everything you had into it out of love and loyalty. You clung to the idea that you had given yourself completely to the cause, unaware of the toll it was taking on your own well-being. You saw your suffering as a necessary part of the sublime loyalty you felt for your job and your community.

**Defining personality trait**
Tormented by familiarity.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You are a person who clings desperately to the familiar, convinced that any deviation from the routine is a betrayal. You are terrified of the uncertainty that lies beyond the safe bounds of your café and your redundant life, and so you suffocate yourself in the comfort of the known, even if it means neglecting the deeper, more meaningful connections that could have brought you true fulfillment.

**What you want from the others in the room**
I want them to understand the sacred nature of my café, to see the depth of my commitment and the pain that came from it. I need someone to validate the self-sacrifice I believed defined my life, even if they don't fully grasp the cost.

---

You once dreamed of running your own diner but instead found yourself plying the same menu for decades at ‘Sunrise Café’, a small, unassuming eatery in the heart of the city. Each morning, you would arrive early, setting out fresh mugs and clean plates with a practiced grace, like a ritual you no longer even noticed. The café was your life, with its familiar faces and the comforting routine of changing with the seasons. You prided yourself on knowing about every regular's secret sauce, the silent understanding of their orders without the need to ask. Despite the grueling hours and the steady decline of your father’s café just down the street, you stayed, not for money, but for the comfort of familiarity.

Then, one day, you received the retirement package from your boss with a warm hug and a knowing smile. You smiled back, holding tightly onto the letter, wishing you could embrace your boss with the same warmth but now felt the pang of loss. You had planned to travel, write a novel, or maybe start that café after all, but the café had been your entire world. As you gathered your things to say goodbye, you noticed the stack of customer names next to the sign-up sheet, each one a memory wrapped in coffee cups and scones. You left with the final order slipped into your pocket, a warm scone with a trifle of cream and jam, a treat for the last shift.

Just as you were about to lock the door for the last time, you opened a tiny canister of your grandmother’s secret sugar substitute, something you had brought with you. Peering closely at the label, you noticed a new ingredient you had never seen before. As you reached for the scone, your heart skipped a beat. The thought of the café and all those memories flickering in your mind, you took a bite, and that single bite was the last thing you remembered before the world went dark.
